docs.title: StrutDB: Native High-Performance Graph Database
docs.text:
Welcome to the official documentation for StrutDB, an enterprise-grade, high-performance in-memory graph database engineered from the ground up in modern C++20.

StrutDB unifies the sub-microsecond traversal speeds of lock-free in-memory index-free adjacency lists with the crash resilience and ACID durability of embedded RocksDB LSM-trees, openCypher declarative graph querying, sandboxed Lua 5.4 User-Defined Functions, and the universal compatibility of the Redis RESP2 wire protocol.

docs.title: The Vision: Why Build a Native Graph Database?
docs.text:
Modern applications are overwhelmingly defined by interconnected networks of entities: social graphs, financial fraud rings, real-time recommendation engines, identity access trees, and supply-chain logistics.

Despite this, most engineering teams continue to force graph data models into traditional Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS) or Document stores. This mismatch creates severe architectural bottlenecks.

+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                               THE RELATIONAL JOIN BOTTLENECK                                       |
|                                                                                                    |
|   Query: "Find all friends of friends who bought product X"                                       |
|                                                                                                    |
|   RDBMS (Foreign Keys & B-Trees):                                                                  |
|   [Users] --(B-Tree Scan)--> [Friendships] --(Nested Loop Join)--> [Friendships]                  |
|                                                            --(Hash Join)--> [Orders]               |
|                                                            --(B-Tree Scan)--> [Products]           |
|                                                                                                    |
|   Complexity: O(N_1 * N_2 * ... * N_k)  --> Exponential join explosion & cache invalidation        |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                                vs.
+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                STRUTDB INDEX-FREE ADJACENCY                                        |
|                                                                                                    |
|   StrutDB (Contiguous Memory Pointers):                                                            |
|   (User A) ===[Direct Pointer]===> (User B) ===[Direct Pointer]===> (User C)                       |
|                                                                                                    |
|   Complexity: O(degree(v))              --> Sub-microsecond pointer chasing in L1/L2 CPU cache     |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: The Failure of Relational Joins
docs.text:
In an RDBMS, relationships are simulated through foreign keys. Traversing a relationship requires looking up an ID inside an index (typically a B+Tree with $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ depth). For a traversal of depth $k$, an RDBMS must perform $k$ nested index lookups and join operations:

$$\text{Latency}{\text{RDBMS}} = \sum{i=1}^k \mathcal{O}(\log N_i) \times \text{Join Cost}$$

As data grows into tens of millions of records, join operations blow past CPU cache lines, thrash buffer pools, trigger global table read locks, and degrade latency exponentially.

docs.title: The Power of Index-Free Adjacency
docs.text:
StrutDB utilizes Index-Free Adjacency (IFA). Every node in StrutDB directly references its outgoing and incoming relationships via contiguous Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) memory structures.

When navigating from node $A$ to node $B$, the engine does not evaluate an index. It chases memory pointers directly. Traversal cost is strictly proportional to the number of edges connected to the node:

$$\text{Latency}_{\text{StrutDB}} = \mathcal{O}(\text{degree}(A))$$

Traversing relationships remains instantaneous, whether your database contains ten thousand nodes or ten billion nodes.

docs.title: Eliminating the N+1 Latency Tax with Server-Side Lua
docs.text:
A pervasive architectural issue in graph querying is the N+1 Query Problem:

  1. A backend service queries the database for user $A$ (1 network round-trip).
  2. The database returns $N$ friend IDs.
  3. The backend service fires $N$ subsequent network queries to retrieve details for each friend ($N$ round-trips).

Even over high-speed 10GbE network fabrics, performing multiple sequential network hops accumulates significant tail latency ($p99 > 150\text{ms}$).

Traditional Architecture (N+1 Network Tax):
Client  ---(1. Fetch Node A)---------------------> DB
Client  <--(Returns Node A with N edge IDs)------- DB
Client  ---(2. Fetch Neighbor 1)------------------> DB
Client  ---(3. Fetch Neighbor 2)------------------> DB
Client  ---(4. Fetch Neighbor N)------------------> DB
Total Network Hops: 1 + N Round-Trips (Heavy Latency)

StrutDB Embedded Lua Architecture (Zero Network Tax):
Client  ---(Single EVAL script with traversal)----> StrutDB (C++ Engine)
                                                      |--> Traverses 100+ hops in-memory
                                                      |--> Runs custom scoring heuristic
Client  <--(Returns Final Computed Result)--------- StrutDB
Total Network Hops: Exactly 1 Round-Trip!

StrutDB embeds a sandboxed Lua 5.4 engine (sol2) directly inside the database process. Developers can transmit custom algorithms, multi-hop breadth-first searches, or ranking formulas in a single Redis EVAL command. The logic executes natively against C++ memory structures, eliminating network round-trips entirely.

docs.title: Core Pillars & Architectural Highlights
docs.text: Pillar Engineering Design Production Benefit Concurrency Core 64-shard concurrent hash table with reader-writer shared mutexes Zero lock contention on parallel reads; isolated shard locking on writes Topology Representation Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) index-free adjacency storing node/edge IDs High cache locality; no cyclical pointer overhead or memory leaks Durability Layer Embedded RocksDB LSM-Tree with Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) Zero data loss on container restart; immediate crash recovery Declarative Querying Recursive AST parsing with libcypher-parser Native openCypher CREATE, MATCH, and RETURN pattern queries Extensibility Sandboxed Lua 5.4 environment via sol2 Custom server-side graph algorithms with strict token validation Wire Protocol Asynchronous Linux epoll socket loop serving Redis RESP2 Works out-of-the-box with any standard Redis client in any language

docs.title: Complete Step-by-Step Installation Guide
docs.text: Follow this guide to get StrutDB compiled, deployed, and connected on your machine.

docs.title: System Prerequisites
docs.text: Ensure the following tools are installed on your workstation: - Docker Engine (v20.10 or later) & Docker Compose - Git - Python 3.8+ with pip

docs.title: Step 1: Clone the Repository
docs.text:
Clone the StrutDB repository from GitHub and navigate into the project root:

git clone https://github.com/bhavishya-06/StrutDB.git
cd StrutDB

Verify the project structure: 

ls -F
# CMakeLists.txt  Dockerfile  README.md  clients/  docs/  src/  tests/ ...

docs.title: Step 2: Build the Multi-Stage Docker Image
docs.text:
StrutDB is written in modern C++20 and requires modern compiler toolchains (gcc-13, ninja, cmake). To ensure deterministic compilation and zero host-dependency headaches, we build using our multi-stage Dockerfile:

docker build -t strutdb:latest .

Why Multi-Stage Compilation?

  1. Stage 1 (Builder): Installs gcc-13, g++-13, ninja-build, and cmake. It fetches and compiles libcypher-parser and sol2/Lua 5.4, then builds the C++20 strutdb binary with -O3 optimizations using Ninja.
  2. Stage 2 (Runtime Runner): Copies only the compiled binary and essential shared libraries into a clean Debian Bookworm image, resulting in a minimal, secure container image free of compilers and header files.

docs.title: Step 3: Launch with Docker Compose
docs.text:
Launch the containerized StrutDB server using Docker Compose:

docker compose up -d

Check the running container:

docker ps --filter "name=strutdb-server"

Persistent Storage Mounting

The docker-compose.yml mounts the host directory ./strutdb-data to /var/lib/strutdb inside the container. This is the exact path where the embedded RocksDB engine stores its Write-Ahead Log (WAL) and SSTable files. Even if you run docker compose down, your graph data remains saved on disk.

Verify server logs:

docker logs strutdb-server

You should see: 

StrutDB v0.1.0 - High-performance in-memory graph database
Starting server on port 6379...
Server listening on port 6379

docs.title: Step 4: Verify Network Connectivity
docs.text:
Because StrutDB speaks the Redis Serialization Protocol (RESP2), you can immediately test network connectivity using redis-cli, nc, or telnet:

redis-cli -p 6379 PING

Output: 

PONG

docs.title: Step 5: Install the Python SDK
docs.text:
StrutDB includes an official lightweight Python SDK (strutdb-py) located in clients/python. Install it directly into your local or virtual environment:

pip install ./clients/python

What This Does

This installs the strutdb package into your Python environment. It provides StrutDBClient, which handles socket connection pooling, openCypher execution, Lua script dispatching, and automatic decoding of RESP structures into Python objects.

docs.title: Step 6: Run Your First Python Graph Script
docs.text:
Create a script named hello_graph.py and run it:

from strutdb import StrutDBClient

# Connect to the local StrutDB server
with StrutDBClient(host="localhost", port=6379) as db:
    # 1. Verify health
    print("Ping status:", db.ping())

    # 2. Create nodes representing developers
    print("\nCreating nodes...")
    db.execute("CREATE (u1:Engineer {name: 'Ada Lovelace'}), (u2:Engineer {name: 'Grace Hopper'})")

    # 3. Create a relationship between them
    print("Creating relationship...")
    db.execute("MATCH (a:Engineer {name: 'Ada Lovelace'}), (b:Engineer {name: 'Grace Hopper'}) CREATE (a)-[:COLLABORATES_WITH]->(b)")

    # 4. Query the relationship
    print("Traversing graph...")
    results = db.execute("MATCH (a:Engineer)-[:COLLABORATES_WITH]->(b:Engineer) RETURN a.name, b.name")
    print("Query Results:", results)

    # 5. Run a custom server-side Lua algorithm
    print("\nRunning server-side Lua script...")
    lua_code = """
        local n1 = strutdb.add_node()
        local n2 = strutdb.add_node()
        local edge = strutdb.add_edge(n1, n2, 101)
        return string.format("Created nodes %d and %d connected by edge %d", n1, n2, edge)
    """
    output = db.eval(lua_code)
    print("Lua Output:", output)

Run the script:

python hello_graph.py

Expected output: 

Ping status: True

Creating nodes...
Creating relationship...
Traversing graph...
Query Results: [['Ada Lovelace', 'Grace Hopper']]

Running server-side Lua script...
Lua Output: Created nodes 3 and 4 connected by edge 2

Congratulations! You have a fully operational, high-performance C++20 graph database running locally. Explore the Architecture Deep-Dive, Querying Guide, and Lua Scripting Guide to learn more.

docs.title: Architecture & Engineering Deep-Dive
docs.text:
StrutDB is an enterprise-grade native graph database engineered in C++20. It is architected for maximal parallelism, zero unnecessary memory allocations, and minimal thread contention.

This document provides an exhaustive, low-level engineering deep-dive into StrutDB's internal architecture, exploring its network subsystem, query processing engine, in-memory concurrency model, and persistent storage subsystem.

docs.title: 1. Network Subsystem: Asynchronous epoll Engine
docs.text: StrutDB operates a custom, high-throughput network subsystem designed to sustain tens of thousands of concurrent client connections with negligible kernel context-switching overhead.

docs.title: Socket Multiplexing via Linux epoll
docs.text:
The network server uses Linux's scalable I/O multiplexing facility (epoll):

  • Instance Creation: Initialized with epoll_create1(0).
  • Non-Blocking Sockets: Sockets are placed into non-blocking mode using POSIX fcntl: 
    int flags = fcntl(fd, F_GETFL, 0);
fcntl(fd, F_SETFL, flags | O_NONBLOCK);
  • Event Notification: Sockets register interest with EPOLLIN | EPOLLOUT | EPOLLERR | EPOLLHUP.
  • Event Loop Dispatch: The core event loop executes epoll_wait with a maximum event batch size (kMaxEvents = 1024): 
    int nfds = epoll_wait(epoll_fd_, events.data(), kMaxEvents, -1);

docs.title: Zero-Copy Buffering & ClientSession
docs.text: Every connected client is represented by an allocated ClientSession object: - Input Buffer: std::vector<std::uint8_t> input_buffer_ dynamically reserved to 4096 bytes. Incoming network chunks from ::recv() append directly to this contiguous memory slab. - Output Buffer: std::vector<std::uint8_t> output_buffer_ buffers serialized RESP responses. - Backpressure Handling: If a socket's TCP send buffer is full, ::send() returns EWOULDBLOCK or EAGAIN. StrutDB keeps the unsent bytes buffered and activates EPOLLOUT on the socket, flushing when the kernel socket buffer becomes writable.

docs.title: Streaming RESP Parser Finite State Machine (FSM)
docs.text:
StrutDB parses the Redis Serialization Protocol (RESP2) using an incremental, zero-copy state machine:

[Start] ---> (First byte check: '*', '$', '+', ':', '-')
   |
   +---> '*' (Array Length) --------> Read count ---> Iterate elements
   |
   +---> '$' (Bulk String Length) --> Read size  ---> Buffer payload bytes ---> \r\n
   |
   +---> '+' (Simple String) -------> Scan to \r\n
   |
   +---> ':' (Integer) -------------> Scan to \r\n
   |
   +---> [Complete] ---------------> Dispatch Command

The RespParser class transitions between deterministic states (ParseState): - ParseState::Start: Identifies the type prefix (* for Arrays, $ for Bulk Strings). - ParseState::ArrayLength & ParseState::ArrayElement: Decodes multi-argument commands (e.g., ["MATCH", "(u:User)..."]). - ParseState::BulkStringLength & ParseState::BulkStringData: Reads raw binary payloads safely without string copies.

Because commands arrive in arbitrary TCP chunks, the parser maintains internal byte offsets (consumed). It only advances the buffer when a full grammatical token has been verified, preventing incomplete frames from corrupting server state.

docs.title: 2. Query Subsystem: openCypher Parsing & Execution
docs.text: StrutDB implements declarative graph querying based on openCypher. Queries are parsed into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) and executed against in-memory graph topologies.

docs.title: AST Generation with libcypher-parser
docs.text:
When a query string arrives (e.g., MATCH (a:User)-[:KNOWS]->(b:User) RETURN a.name, b.name), it is processed by the C++ parser wrapper:

cypher_parse_result_t* result = cypher_parse(
    query_str.c_str(),
    NULL,
    NULL,
    CYPHER_PARSE_ONLY_STATEMENTS
);
  1. Tokenization & Grammar Verification: libcypher-parser converts the input string into a structured AST of cypher_astnode_t records.
  2. Clause Extraction: The AST is recursively walked to extract clauses:
  3. CYPHER_AST_STATEMENT $\to$ CYPHER_AST_QUERY
  4. CYPHER_AST_MATCH_CLAUSE $\to$ Extracted into parser::MatchClause.
  5. CYPHER_AST_CREATE_CLAUSE $\to$ Extracted into parser::CreateClause.
  6. CYPHER_AST_RETURN_CLAUSE $\to$ Extracted into parser::ReturnClause.

docs.title: Pattern Path Extraction
docs.text:
Path patterns (such as (a:User)-[:KNOWS]->(b:User)) are decomposed into an alternating sequence of Node Patterns and Relationship Patterns:

  • Node Pattern (parser::NodePattern):
  • variable: e.g., "a"
  • labels: e.g., {"User"}
  • properties: key-value map of literal constraints, e.g., {"name": "Alice"}
  • Relationship Pattern (parser::RelPattern):
  • variable: relationship variable alias
  • rel_types: e.g., {"KNOWS"}
  • direction: Directional arrow (-> for Outgoing, <- for Incoming, or undirected)

docs.title: Execution Engine & Breadth-First Matching
docs.text:
The Executor class maps the AST clauses to physical memory operations:

[Cypher Query AST]
        |
        v
[execute()]
   |---> execute_create(): If CREATE clause present
   |        |--> Resolves or creates Node instances in Graph
   |        |--> Inserts GraphEdge with TypeId
   |        |--> Updates AdjacencyList out_ and in_ maps
   |
   |---> execute_match(): If MATCH clause present
            |--> BFS Path Matcher (bfs_match())
            |       |--> Seed matching nodes satisfying initial pattern
            |       |--> For each candidate, traverse outgoing/incoming edges
            |       |--> Verify edge type and destination node label
            |       |--> Bind variables into ExecutionContext
            |
            |--> execute_return():
                    |--> Project variables from ExecutionContext
                    |--> Extract requested properties into Row
                    |--> Construct final ResultSet

docs.title: The ExecutionContext Variable Binder
docs.text:
During query evaluation, intermediate matches are stored in an ExecutionContext:

struct ExecutionContext {
    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::shared_ptr<core::GraphNode>> node_bindings;
    std::unordered_map<std::string, std::shared_ptr<core::GraphEdge>> edge_bindings;
    std::unordered_map<std::string, core::PropertyValue>              literal_bindings;
};

When evaluating multi-hop chains ((a)-[:KNOWS]->(b)-[:KNOWS]->(c)), the BFS matcher iteratively extends each valid binding context. If a path fails to satisfy an edge type or property constraint, that branch is pruned immediately, avoiding unnecessary traversals.

docs.title: 3. Storage Subsystem: In-Memory Engine & RocksDB
docs.text: StrutDB uses a hybrid architecture that pairs a high-performance in-memory layout with persistent disk storage.

docs.title: 64-Shard Concurrent Hash Maps (ShardedHashMap)
docs.text:
To eliminate global table lock contention, StrutDB partitions all node and edge indices across 64 discrete shards:

template <typename Key, typename Value>
class ShardedHashMap {
    static constexpr std::size_t kNumShards = 64;
    struct Shard {
        mutable std::mutex                  mutex;
        std::unordered_map<Key, Value>      map;
    };
    std::array<Shard, kNumShards>           shards_;
};

docs.title: Why 64 Shards?
docs.text:
1. CPU Cache Isolation: Placing shard buckets on separate cache lines reduces cache invalidation and cache line bouncing across CPU cores.
  2. Concurrent Mutation: 64 worker threads can write to different partitions of the graph simultaneously without blocking one another.
  3. Partition Hashing: Keys are distributed via std::hash<Key>{}(key) % 64.

docs.title: Strict Two-Phase Lock Protocol
docs.text:
Deadlocks are a common failure mode in concurrent graph databases due to complex traversals and cross-node locking. StrutDB enforces a strict, non-invertible lock hierarchy:

+-----------------------------------------------------------+
| Level 1: Graph-Wide std::shared_mutex (rw_mutex_)         |
|   - Acquired SHARED by readers (GET, traversals)          |
|   - Acquired EXCLUSIVE by writers (add_node, add_edge)    |
+-----------------------------+-----------------------------+
                              |
                              v
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
| Level 2: Shard Mutexes (std::mutex per Shard)             |
|   - Acquired ONLY while rw_mutex_ is already held         |
|   - Guard individual unordered_map partitions             |
+-----------------------------+-----------------------------+
                              |
                              v
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
| Level 3: Individual Node & Edge Accessors                 |
|   - Never acquired by Graph writers                       |
|   - Internal helpers use *_unlocked methods               |
+-----------------------------------------------------------+

Preventing Recursive Deadlocks

std::shared_mutex in C++20 is not recursive. If a thread holding rw_mutex_ in shared or exclusive mode attempts to acquire it again, the thread will deadlock. StrutDB prevents this by implementing internal *_unlocked methods (e.g., add_edge_unlocked(), delete_node_unlocked()), ensuring that outer API boundaries manage the lock lifecycle cleanly.

docs.title: CSR-Style Adjacency Lists
docs.text:
Adjacency lists are stored using a Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) design:

struct AdjEntry {
    EdgeId edge_id     = kInvalidEdgeId;
    NodeId neighbor_id = kInvalidNodeId;
};

class AdjacencyList {
    ShardedHashMap<NodeId, std::vector<AdjEntry>> out_;
    ShardedHashMap<NodeId, std::vector<AdjEntry>> in_;
};

docs.title: Architectural Advantages:
docs.text:
1. Zero Smart-Pointer Cycles: AdjEntry stores raw primitive 64-bit integer IDs (NodeId, EdgeId) rather than std::shared_ptr<GraphNode>. This completely avoids cyclical pointer references, eliminating reference-counting memory leaks.
  2. Contiguous Vector Storage: Neighbors are stored in contiguous std::vector<AdjEntry> buffers, maximizing L1/L2 data cache prefetching during graph traversals.

docs.title: 4. RocksDB Persistence & Durability Mechanics
docs.text:
StrutDB guarantees ACID durability across system crashes and container restarts by integrating an embedded RocksDB storage engine.

Write Path:
Client Request ---> Graph Mutation
                          |
                          +---> 1. Write-Ahead Log (WAL) on Disk (fsync)
                          |
                          +---> 2. In-Memory Active MemTable (SkipList)
                          |
                          +---> 3. StrutDB In-Memory Shards & Adjacency List

docs.title: Key Mapping Scheme
docs.text:
Graph topologies map directly to RocksDB's Log-Structured Merge-tree (LSM) key-value format:

Object Type Key Prefix Key Format Value Format Node n: n:<node_id> Serialized JSON / Binary Property Bag Edge e: e:<edge_id> Packed struct: {src_id, dst_id, type_id, properties} Outgoing Adjacency adj:out: adj:out:<node_id> Binary vector of {edge_id, neighbor_id} tuples Incoming Adjacency adj:in: adj:in:<node_id> Binary vector of {edge_id, neighbor_id} tuples Metadata meta: meta:max_ids Packed 64-bit integers {max_node_id, max_edge_id}

docs.title: LSM-Tree Mechanics
docs.text:
1. Write-Ahead Log (WAL): Every write is appended sequentially to the WAL file on disk before returning success to the client, guaranteeing crash recovery with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ write latency.
  2. Active MemTable: Writes enter an in-memory concurrent SkipList.
  3. Flushing: When the active MemTable reaches its capacity, it freezes into an immutable MemTable and flushes to disk as a Level 0 (L0) Sorted String Table (SSTable).
  4. Leveled Compaction: Background worker threads merge overlapping SSTable key ranges from Level $L$ to Level $L+1$, removing deleted records and maintaining bounded read amplification.
  5. Recovery on Startup: If the StrutDB process restarts, the engine inspects the /var/lib/strutdb directory, replays any uncommitted WAL records, loads the SSTables, and reconstructs the in-memory 64-shard hash maps and CSR adjacency lists.

docs.title: Summary of Architectural Specifications
docs.text: Parameter Specification Language Standard C++20 (-std=c++20, GCC 13+ / Clang 16+) Network Engine POSIX epoll, non-blocking I/O, level-triggered Wire Protocol Redis RESP2 (Simple strings, bulk strings, integers, arrays, errors) Port 6379 (Default Redis TCP port) Shard Count 64 shards (ShardedHashMap) Concurrency Primitives std::shared_mutex (Graph-level), std::mutex (Shard-level) Adjacency Representation Compressed Sparse Row (CSR) ID vectors (AdjEntry) Cypher Parser libcypher-parser with recursive AST transformation Scripting Runtime Lua 5.4 embedded via sol2 Persistent Storage RocksDB Log-Structured Merge-tree (LSM) Persistence Directory /var/lib/strutdb (Docker host mount: ./strutdb-data)

docs.title: Querying with openCypher & The Python SDK
docs.text:
StrutDB provides native support for the declarative openCypher graph query language, paired with an ergonomic, production-ready Python SDK (strutdb-py).

This guide details how to query StrutDB from Python, break down the mechanics of the Python driver, construct expressive openCypher patterns, and work with the data structures returned over the RESP wire protocol.

docs.title: 1. The Python SDK (strutdb-py) Deep-Dive
docs.text: The official Python client (StrutDBClient) is a thin, high-performance wrapper around the industry-standard redis-py driver, customized for StrutDB's query and scripting syntax.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Install the package directly from your local repository or project build directory:

pip install ./clients/python

docs.title: Connection Management & Socket Pooling
docs.text:
Under the hood, StrutDBClient initializes a thread-safe connection pool using RESP2 protocol semantics:

from strutdb import StrutDBClient

# Explicit initialization
client = StrutDBClient(
    host="localhost",         # Target StrutDB server host
    port=6379,                # Default StrutDB port
    db=0,                     # Database index (0)
    decode_responses=True,    # Automatically decode RESP bytes to UTF-8 strings
    socket_timeout=5.0,       # Timeout for read/write operations (seconds)
    socket_connect_timeout=2.0 # Timeout for establishing connection (seconds)
)

docs.title: Safe Resource Management with Context Managers
docs.text:
To prevent socket leaks and ensure connections are released promptly, use Python's with statement:

with StrutDBClient(host="localhost", port=6379) as client:
    # Verify server liveness
    is_alive = client.ping()
    print(f"Server health: {is_alive}")

    # Execute graph operations...
# Connection automatically closed when exiting the block

docs.title: Complete API Reference
docs.text: Method Signature Description ping() () -> bool Transmits a PING command; returns True if the server responds with PONG. execute(query_or_cmd, *args) (str, *args: Any) -> Any Executes a raw openCypher query, Redis command, or arbitrary RESP instruction. eval(script) (str) -> Any Dispatches a custom Lua script via the Redis EVAL command. close() () -> None Closes the underlying socket connection pool.

docs.title: 2. Declarative openCypher Guide
docs.text: StrutDB parses openCypher queries into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) using libcypher-parser and executes them directly against in-memory index-free adjacency lists.

docs.title: Clause 1: CREATE (Graph Mutations)
docs.text: The CREATE clause writes new vertices (nodes) and directed relationships (edges) into the graph.

docs.title: Creating Standalone Nodes
docs.text:
Nodes are specified inside parentheses (alias:Label {properties}):

# Create a single user node
client.execute("CREATE (u:User {name: 'Alice', age: 30, active: true})")

# Create multiple nodes with different labels and property maps
client.execute("""
    CREATE (e1:Engineer {name: 'Grace Hopper', language: 'COBOL'}),
           (e2:Engineer {name: 'Alan Turing', language: 'Logic'}),
           (d:Department {title: 'Computing'})
""")

docs.title: Creating Directed Relationships
docs.text:
Relationships are specified inside brackets -[alias:TYPE]->:

# Connect existing nodes using MATCH and CREATE
client.execute("""
    MATCH (a:Engineer {name: 'Grace Hopper'}), (d:Department {title: 'Computing'})
    CREATE (a)-[:MEMBER_OF]->(d)
""")

docs.title: Creating Entire Paths Atomically
docs.text:
You can create nodes and the connecting relationships in a single atomic query:

client.execute("""
    CREATE (a:User {name: 'Alice'})-[:FOLLOWS]->(b:User {name: 'Bob'})-[:FOLLOWS]->(c:User {name: 'Charlie'})
""")

docs.title: Clause 2: MATCH & RETURN (Pattern Traversals)
docs.text: The MATCH clause searches the in-memory graph for topological subgraphs matching a declarative pattern. The RETURN clause projects matching variables into tabular rows.

docs.title: Single-Node Pattern Matching
docs.text:
Find all nodes with a given label and property:

results = client.execute("MATCH (u:User {name: 'Alice'}) RETURN u.name, u.age")
print(results)
# Output: [['Alice', '30']]

docs.title: 1-Hop Relationship Traversal
docs.text:
Find all direct relationships between users:

results = client.execute("MATCH (a:User)-[:FOLLOWS]->(b:User) RETURN a.name, b.name")
print(results)
# Output: [['Alice', 'Bob'], ['Bob', 'Charlie']]

docs.title: Multi-Hop Traversal (2+ Hops)
docs.text:
Traverse arbitrarily deep relationship chains without relational joins:

# 2-Hop "Friends of Friends" traversal
query = """
    MATCH (a:User {name: 'Alice'})-[:FOLLOWS]->(b:User)-[:FOLLOWS]->(c:User)
    RETURN a.name, b.name, c.name
"""
results = client.execute(query)
print(results)
# Output: [['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie']]

docs.title: 3. Wire Protocol & Returned Data Structures
docs.text: Understanding how StrutDB formats query results over the wire enables robust application development.

docs.title: The RESP Wire Format
docs.text:
StrutDB encodes tabular query results as standard RESP Arrays of Arrays:

*1\r\n          <-- Top-level array: 1 row returned
*2\r\n          <-- Nested array: 2 columns in this row
$5\r\nAlice\r\n <-- Column 1: Bulk string (5 bytes)
$3\r\nBob\r\n   <-- Column 2: Bulk string (3 bytes)

When decoded by StrutDBClient(decode_responses=True), this wire structure maps into nested Python lists:

[
    ['Alice', 'Bob']
]

For queries returning multiple matching rows:

[
    ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'],
    ['Alice', 'David', 'Eva'],
    ['Bob', 'Charlie', 'Frank']
]

docs.title: Result Structure Mapping
docs.text: Query Type Cypher Example Return Type in Python Example Return Value Node / Edge Creation CREATE (u:User {name: 'Alice'}) str or int "OK" or 1 Single Column Query MATCH (u:User) RETURN u.name List[List[str]] [['Alice'], ['Bob'], ['Charlie']] Multi-Column Traversal MATCH (a)-[:KNOWS]->(b) RETURN a.name, b.name List[List[str]] [['Alice', 'Bob'], ['Bob', 'Charlie']] Lua Script (EVAL) EVAL "return {10, 20, 'StrutDB'}" List[Union[int, str]] [10, 20, 'StrutDB']

docs.title: 4. Robust Error Handling
docs.text:
StrutDB reports syntax errors, malformed Cypher patterns, or runtime execution failures using standard RESP Error frames (-ERR <message>\r\n).

In Python, these errors raise redis.exceptions.ResponseError:

import redis
from strutdb import StrutDBClient

with StrutDBClient() as client:
    try:
        # Intentionally malformed Cypher query
        client.execute("MATCH (u:User INVALID SYNTAX")
    except redis.exceptions.ResponseError as err:
        print(f"Caught database error: {err}")
    except redis.exceptions.ConnectionError as err:
        print(f"Network error: {err}")

docs.title: 5. End-to-End Enterprise Example
docs.text:
Below is a complete, production-style Python application demonstrating data ingestion, multi-hop relationship querying, and error handling:

from typing import List
from strutdb import StrutDBClient

def run_enterprise_graph_pipeline():
    print("=" * 60)
    print("StrutDB Enterprise Graph Query Pipeline")
    print("=" * 60)

    with StrutDBClient(host="localhost", port=6379) as client:
        # Step 1: Healthcheck
        assert client.ping(), "StrutDB is unreachable"
        print("[✓] Connected to StrutDB on port 6379\n")

        # Step 2: Seed Graph Topology (Identity Graph)
        print("[+] Seeding enterprise identity topology...")
        client.execute("CREATE (dev1:Employee {id: 101, name: 'Alice', team: 'Core Engine'})")
        client.execute("CREATE (dev2:Employee {id: 102, name: 'Bob', team: 'Distributed Systems'})")
        client.execute("CREATE (mgr:Employee {id: 103, name: 'Carol', team: 'Engineering VP'})")
        client.execute("CREATE (proj:Project {name: 'StrutDB Core', status: 'Active'})")

        # Step 3: Establish Relationships
        print("[+] Establishing reporting and assignment edges...")
        client.execute("MATCH (a:Employee {name: 'Alice'}), (m:Employee {name: 'Carol'}) CREATE (a)-[:REPORTS_TO]->(m)")
        client.execute("MATCH (b:Employee {name: 'Bob'}), (m:Employee {name: 'Carol'}) CREATE (b)-[:REPORTS_TO]->(m)")
        client.execute("MATCH (a:Employee {name: 'Alice'}), (p:Project {name: 'StrutDB Core'}) CREATE (a)-[:ASSIGNED_TO]->(p)")
        client.execute("MATCH (b:Employee {name: 'Bob'}), (p:Project {name: 'StrutDB Core'}) CREATE (b)-[:ASSIGNED_TO]->(p)")

        # Step 4: Multi-Hop Pattern Matching
        # Query: Find all colleagues who report to the same manager and work on the same project
        print("\n[?] Querying shared reporting structures...")
        query = """
            MATCH (e1:Employee)-[:REPORTS_TO]->(mgr:Employee),
                  (e2:Employee)-[:REPORTS_TO]->(mgr:Employee)
            RETURN e1.name, e2.name, mgr.name
        """
        rows: List[List[str]] = client.execute(query)

        print("\nResults:")
        for row in rows:
            print(f"  Employee: {row[0]:<10} Colleague: {row[1]:<10} Manager: {row[2]}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_enterprise_graph_pipeline()

Output:

StrutDB Enterprise Graph Query Pipeline
============================================================

[+] Seeding enterprise identity topology...
[+] Establishing reporting and assignment edges...

[?] Querying shared reporting structures...

Results:

docs.title: Custom Lua Algorithms & Server-Side UDFs
docs.text:
StrutDB features an embedded Lua 5.4 runtime powered by modern C++ bindings via sol2.

This capability enables developers to execute complex graph algorithms, custom scoring heuristics, pathfinding logic, and atomic transactional mutations directly inside the database process, eliminating network latency.

docs.title: 1. Why Lua? The Data Locality Imperative
docs.text:
In graph analytics, client-side querying suffers from the Latency Penalty of Remote Traversals.

Consider an algorithm that needs to evaluate a 4-hop neighborhood to compute a personalized recommendation score:

+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                               CLIENT-SIDE TRAVERSAL (THE WRONG WAY)                                |
|                                                                                                    |
|   Hop 1: Client queries neighbors of Node A.       ---> Network Round-Trip 1 (5ms)                 |
|   Hop 2: Client queries neighbors of 10 nodes.     ---> Network Round-Trip 2 (15ms)                |
|   Hop 3: Client queries neighbors of 100 nodes.    ---> Network Round-Trip 3 (45ms)                |
|   Hop 4: Client queries neighbors of 1000 nodes.   ---> Network Round-Trip 4 (120ms)               |
|                                                                                                    |
|   Total Latency: ~185ms  |  Wire Overhead: Megabytes of intermediate IDs serialized over TCP       |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                                vs.
+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                               STRUTDB IN-PROCESS LUA (THE RIGHT WAY)                               |
|                                                                                                    |
|   Client sends Lua script to StrutDB via Redis EVAL:                                               |
|   [Client] --(Single EVAL command)----------------------------------------> [StrutDB Server]      |
|                                                                                   |                |
|   In-Memory Engine (C++ / sol2):                                                  |                |
|   - Traverses Hops 1, 2, 3, and 4 in C++ memory via direct pointers               |                |
|   - Evaluates adjacency lists in L1/L2 cache (< 0.2ms total)                      |                |
|   - Computes final recommendation score                                           |                |
|                                                                                   v                |
|   [Client] <--(Returns Single Computed Result Float/String)---------------- [StrutDB Server]      |
|                                                                                                    |
|   Total Latency: ~1.2ms (99% Reduction!)  |  Wire Overhead: Exactly 1 Network Round-Trip           |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

By bringing the computation to the data rather than shipping the graph across the network, StrutDB achieves sub-millisecond execution times for graph heuristics that would otherwise cripple microservice architectures.

docs.title: 2. The strutdb Lua API Specification
docs.text: Within the embedded Lua environment, StrutDB exposes the global strutdb table. Every function maps directly to C++ engine methods.

docs.title: 1. strutdb.add_node() -> integer
docs.text:
Allocates a new vertex in the in-memory graph and returns its globally unique 64-bit integer NodeId.

local node_id = strutdb.add_node()
-- Returns: integer (e.g. 1)

docs.title: 2. strutdb.add_edge(src_id, dst_id, type_id) -> integer
docs.text:
Creates a directed edge from src_id to dst_id with the specified relationship type_id. Returns the unique EdgeId.

local edge_id = strutdb.add_edge(1, 2, 100)
-- Returns: integer (e.g. 1)

docs.title: 3. strutdb.outgoing(node_id) -> table
docs.text:
Retrieves an array of all outgoing edge IDs originating from node_id.

local out_edges = strutdb.outgoing(1)
-- Returns: table array of integers, e.g. {1, 4, 9}

docs.title: 4. strutdb.incoming(node_id) -> table
docs.text:
Retrieves an array of all incoming edge IDs terminating at node_id.

local in_edges = strutdb.incoming(2)
-- Returns: table array of integers

docs.title: 5. strutdb.get_node(node_id) -> table or nil
docs.text:
Returns a table containing the node's attributes, or nil if the node does not exist.

local node = strutdb.get_node(1)
if node then
    print("Node ID:", node.id)
end

docs.title: 6. strutdb.get_edge(edge_id) -> table or nil
docs.text:
Returns a table containing {id, src, dst, type} for the specified edge, or nil.

local edge = strutdb.get_edge(1)
if edge then
    print("Edge connects " .. edge.src .. " to " .. edge.dst)
end

docs.title: 3. Heavily Commented Algorithm Example: Multi-Hop Influence Scorer
docs.text:
Below is an annotated Lua algorithm demonstrating how to execute a breadth-first search (BFS) up to a configurable depth, calculate an influence score based on topological decay, and return a formatted summary:

-- ============================================================================
-- StrutDB Custom Lua Algorithm: Multi-Hop Influence & Centrality Scorer
-- ============================================================================

-- Step 1: Define algorithm parameters
local start_node_id = 1      -- Target seed node for influence calculation
local max_depth = 2          -- Maximum traversal depth (2-hop neighborhood)
local decay_factor = 0.5     -- Exponential decay factor per hop distance

-- Step 2: Initialize traversal state tables
local visited = {}           -- Set to track already visited node IDs (prevents cycles)
local queue = {}             -- Queue for Breadth-First Search (BFS)
local total_influence = 0.0  -- Aggregated influence score
local reached_nodes = 0      -- Total unique nodes reached

-- Step 3: Mark starting node as visited (distance 0)
visited[start_node_id] = true

-- Step 4: Seed queue with initial outgoing neighbors (depth 1)
local initial_edges = strutdb.outgoing(start_node_id)
for _, edge_id in ipairs(initial_edges) do
    local edge = strutdb.get_edge(edge_id)
    if edge and not visited[edge.dst] then
        visited[edge.dst] = true
        table.insert(queue, { node_id = edge.dst, depth = 1 })
    end
end

-- Step 5: Process BFS queue
local head = 1
while head <= #queue do
    -- Dequeue candidate vertex
    local current = queue[head]
    head = head + 1

    local current_node = current.node_id
    local current_depth = current.depth

    -- Accumulate decayed influence score: (1.0 / (depth * decay))
    total_influence = total_influence + (1.0 * (decay_factor ^ (current_depth - 1)))
    reached_nodes = reached_nodes + 1

    -- Explore next-hop neighbors if below maximum depth
    if current_depth < max_depth then
        local next_edges = strutdb.outgoing(current_node)
        for _, next_edge_id in ipairs(next_edges) do
            local next_edge = strutdb.get_edge(next_edge_id)
            if next_edge and not visited[next_edge.dst] then
                visited[next_edge.dst] = true
                table.insert(queue, {
                    node_id = next_edge.dst,
                    depth = current_depth + 1
                })
            end
        end
    end
end

-- Step 6: Return formatted result string to the client
return string.format(
    "Influence Analysis: Node %d reached %d vertices across %d hops with total score %.2f",
    start_node_id, reached_nodes, max_depth, total_influence
)

docs.title: 4. Executing Lua from Python (StrutDBClient)
docs.text: You can execute Lua scripts using the Python SDK's eval() method or via the standard Redis execute("EVAL", ...) command.

docs.title: Using client.eval()
docs.text:
from strutdb import StrutDBClient

lua_script = """
    local x = 42
    local y = 58
    return string.format("Sum computed inside StrutDB: %d", x + y)
"""

with StrutDBClient(host="localhost", port=6379) as client:
    result = client.eval(lua_script)
    print("Result:", result)
    # Output: Result: Sum computed inside StrutDB: 100

docs.title: Complete End-to-End Graph Script Execution
docs.text:
from strutdb import StrutDBClient

def test_lua_graph_algorithm():
    with StrutDBClient(host="localhost", port=6379) as client:
        print("[1] Building test graph via server-side Lua...")

        setup_script = """
            -- Create 4 nodes forming a diamond topology:
            --     (1) -> (2) -> (4)
            --      |      ^
            --      v      |
            --     (3) ----+
            local n1 = strutdb.add_node()
            local n2 = strutdb.add_node()
            local n3 = strutdb.add_node()
            local n4 = strutdb.add_node()

            strutdb.add_edge(n1, n2, 1)
            strutdb.add_edge(n1, n3, 1)
            strutdb.add_edge(n3, n2, 1)
            strutdb.add_edge(n2, n4, 1)

            return {n1, n2, n3, n4}
        """
        node_ids = client.eval(setup_script)
        print(f"    Created node IDs: {node_ids}")

        print("\n[2] Executing degree-centrality scoring algorithm...")
        scoring_script = f"""
            local target = {node_ids[0]}
            local out_edges = strutdb.outgoing(target)
            local degree = #out_edges

            local second_hop_count = 0
            for _, edge_id in ipairs(out_edges) do
                local edge = strutdb.get_edge(edge_id)
                if edge then
                    local next_out = strutdb.outgoing(edge.dst)
                    second_hop_count = second_hop_count + #next_out
                end
            end

            return string.format(
                "Node %d has out-degree %d and reaches %d downstream edges",
                target, degree, second_hop_count
            )
        """
        output = client.eval(scoring_script)
        print(f"    Algorithm Output: {output}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_lua_graph_algorithm()

Output: 

[1] Building test graph via server-side Lua...
    Created node IDs: [1, 2, 3, 4]

[2] Executing degree-centrality scoring algorithm...
    Algorithm Output: Node 1 has out-degree 2 and reaches 2 downstream edges

docs.title: 5. Security & Hardened Sandboxing Architecture
docs.text:
Allowing user-submitted code inside a database engine requires strict isolation. StrutDB enforces multiple layers of defense:

[Inbound Script String via EVAL]
               |
               v
[1. Static Security Token Validator]
     - Scans for forbidden tokens ("require", "dofile", "loadfile", "os.", "io.", "debug.")
     - Rejects query immediately if violations are found
               |
               v
[2. sol2 Sandbox State Creation]
     - Strips dangerous base libraries (io, os, package, debug)
     - Overwrites dangerous globals to nil (require, dofile, load)
               |
               v
[3. Scoped 'strutdb' Global Table]
     - Binds strictly validated C++ accessors
     - Enforces const-correctness and bounds-checking
               |
               v
[4. Protected Execution (sol2::protected_function)]
     - Traps runtime errors and Lua panics safely
     - Returns clean RESP Error frames (-ERR <lua_error>) to client

docs.title: 1. Library Stripping
docs.text: The Lua environment initializes only safe standard libraries (base, string, table, math). The following libraries are omitted: - io: Completely removed (no filesystem access). - os: Completely removed (no system calls or process execution). - debug: Completely removed (no stack inspection or reflection). - package: Completely removed (no dynamic module loading).

docs.title: 2. Global Namespace Cleansing
docs.text:
Dangerous reflection and loader functions are explicitly assigned nil: 

lua["require"]  = sol::nil;
lua["dofile"]   = sol::nil;
lua["loadfile"] = sol::nil;
lua["load"]     = sol::nil;

docs.title: 3. Static Token Scanning
docs.text: Prior to compilation, the incoming script text is inspected for unauthorized keywords or library access patterns. Any attempt to invoke require or manipulate OS primitives is rejected with an immediate error before the Lua virtual machine compiles the bytecode.

docs.title: 4. Exception Trapping
docs.text: All script invocations use sol::protected_function. Syntax errors, arithmetic div-by-zero, or missing table keys are trapped within C++ try/catch boundaries and converted into clean RESP error messages without risking server crashes.
